key_big: Value after n years = start × multiplierⁿ.
key_sub: A 4% increase is × 1.04. A 15% decrease is × 0.85.
body_html:
How it works

A multiplier changes an amount by a percentage in one step. A 4% increase is × 1.04; a 15% decrease is × 0.85.

Compound interest is interest added to the total each year, so next year's interest is bigger. Value after n years = start × multipliern. The same idea works for depreciation (a falling value) and for populations that grow or shrink by a percentage.

Example

£2,000 at 3% compound interest for 2 years.

Multiplier 1.03.

2000 × 1.032 = 2121.80.

Answer: £2,121.80

Example

A £12,000 car loses 20% a year. Value after 3 years?

Multiplier 0.8.

12000 × 0.83 = 6144.

Answer: £6,144

Example

Compare with 3% simple interest on £2,000 for 2 years.

£60 a year, × 2 = £120.

Answer: £2,120 (less than compound)

Common mistakes

  • Using simple interest when the question says compound.
  • Writing 1.5 for a 5% increase. 5% is 0.05, so the multiplier is 1.05.
  • Giving the interest when the question asks for the total, or the total when it asks for the interest.
  • Multiplying by the multiplier × the number of years (1.03 × 4) instead of using a power (1.034).

faq.q: What is the formula for compound interest?
faq.a: Amount = start × (1 + r/100)ⁿ, where r is the interest rate and n is the number of years. For 3% for 5 years, multiply by 1.03⁵.

faq.q: What is the difference between simple and compound interest?
faq.a: Simple interest pays the same amount every year, based on the start amount. Compound interest pays interest on the interest too, so it grows faster.
A loss in value over time. If a car loses 20% a year, multiply by 0.8 for each year.

faq.q: How do I find a multiplier?
faq.a: For an increase add the percentage to 100%; for a decrease subtract it. Then divide by 100: 7% increase is 1.07, 7% decrease is 0.93.

Which gives more money after 2 years on £1,000: 5% simple interest or 5% compound interest?
items.e: Simple: £1,100. Compound: £1,000 × 1.052 = £1,102.50. Compound interest gives more, because interest is earned on interest.

Which calculation gives the value of £600 after 4 years at 3% compound interest?
items.e: The multiplier is 1.03, used once for each year: 600 × 1.034.

items.q: Which calculation gives the value of a £9,000 car after 5 years if it loses 15% each year?
items.e: Losing 15% leaves 85%, so the multiplier is 0.85: 9000 × 0.855.

items.q: A house is worth £200,000. Its value rises 10% one year then falls 10% the next. What is it worth now?
items.e: £200,000 × 1.1 × 0.9 = £198,000. The 10% fall is of a bigger amount.
